editorial_contributions.text:
An algorithm is proposed for the hypergeometric distribution and generalizations and limiting cases thereof: binomial, Poisson, Pascal \((=negative\) binomial), geometric, rectangular, and many more ``similar'' ones as e.g. logarithmic series, hyper-Poisson, Polya-Eggenberger. 


It is the rejection algorithm for generating random variates in the cases, when the distribution is discrete univariate, unimodal and not feasibly invertible (by computation), but closely majorized by an easily computable function g(k). Considered are distributions \(p_ k\) (k\(\in {\mathbb{Z}})\) with log \(p_ k\) concave and therefore of limited variance in k (uniformly), which covers the above mentioned distributions. In this case g(k) can be a constant or simple stepwise exponentially) decreasing function, i.e.: \(g(k)=c\cdot e^{-a| m-k|}\) for k outside the range of the modes (points with maximal probability, m one of them, c depending on the sign of m-k). On the other hand, for the rejection algorithm, the expected number of trials turns out to be \(4+p_ m\) (less in special cases), where \(p_ m\) is the probability of a mode. 


The algorithm itself is a simple program of a few lines - besides using a call for the actual distribution function - consisting of usual arithmetic, a call for the exponential (as being the principal part of the majoriser), three calls for generating independent random variables (uniform in 0...1), a call for a random sign \((+/-)\), and a combination of comparisons as rejection condition; all this for each trial. 


The performance depends on the closeness of g(k) to the actual distribution and is not discussed.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: In the multidimensional 0-1 knapsack problem, we are given a set of items, each with a value and multiple attributes, and we want to select a subset in such a way that the total value is maximized while the total quantity of each attribute satisfies a capacity constraint. In this paper, we assume that quantities of the item attributes are independent random variables such that those of the same attribute across different items follow the same type of probability distribution, not necessarily with the same parameters. A joint probabilistic constraint is imposed on the capacity constraints, and the objective function is the same as that of the underlying deterministic problem. We prove that the problem is convex, under some condition on the parameters, for special continuous and discrete distributions: gamma, normal, Poisson, and binomial, in which the latter two discrete distribution functions are extended to log-concave continuous distribution functions. We present computational experiments to demonstrate the tractability of our approach.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: We study the question of testing structured properties (classes) of discrete distributions. Specifically, given sample access to an arbitrary distribution \(D\) over \([n]\) and a property \({\mathcal P}\), the goal is to distinguish between \(D\in{\mathcal P}\) and \(\ell_1(D,{\mathcal P})>\varepsilon\). We develop a general algorithm for this question, which applies to a large range of ``shape-constrained'' properties, including monotone, log-concave, \(t\)-modal, piecewise-polynomial, and Poisson Binomial distributions. Moreover, for all cases considered, our algorithm has near-optimal sample complexity with regard to the domain size and is computationally efficient. For most of these classes, we provide the first non-trivial tester in the literature. In addition, we also describe a generic method to prove lower bounds for this problem, and use it to show our upper bounds are nearly tight. Finally, we extend some of our techniques to tolerant testing, deriving nearly-tight upper and lower bounds for the corresponding questions.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1338.68009].

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: We give a computationally efficient semi-agnostic algorithm for learning univariate probability distributions that are well approximated by piecewise polynomial density functions. Let \(p\) be an arbitrary distribution over an interval \(I\), and suppose that \(p\) is \(\tau\)-close (in total variation distance) to an unknown probability distribution \(q\) that is defined by an unknown partition of \(I\) into \(t\) intervals and \(t\) unknown degree \(d\) polynomials specifying \(q\) over each of the intervals. We give an algorithm that draws \(\tilde{O}(t(d + 1)/\varepsilon^{2})\) samples from \(p\), runs in time \(\operatorname{poly}(t, d + 1, 1/\varepsilon)\), and with high probability outputs a piecewise polynomial hypothesis distribution \(h\) that is \((14\tau + \varepsilon)\)-close to \(p\) in total variation distance. Our algorithm combines tools from real approximation theory, uniform convergence, linear programming, and dynamic programming. Its sample complexity is simultaneously near optimal in all three parameters \(t\), \(d\) and \(\varepsilon\); we show that even for \(\tau = 0\), any algorithm that learns an unknown \(t\)-piecewise degree-\(d\) probability distribution over \(I\) to accuracy \(\varepsilon\) must use \(\Omega\left(\frac{t(d+1)}{\operatorname{poly}(\log(d+2))} \cdot \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\) samples from the distribution, regardless of its running time.

 We apply this general algorithm to obtain a wide range of results for many natural density estimation problems over both continuous and discrete domains. These include state-of-the-art results for learning mixtures of log-concave distributions; mixtures of \(t\)-modal distributions; mixtures of Monotone Hazard Rate distributions; mixtures of Poisson Binomial Distributions; mixtures of Gaussians; and mixtures of \(k\)-monotone densities. Our general technique gives improved results, with provably optimal sample complexities (up to logarithmic factors) in all parameters in most cases, for all these problems via a single unified algorithm.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1294.68009].

title.title: Quantitative limit theorems via relative log-concavity

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Ultra-log-concave distributions are ubiquitous in probability, combinatorics, and statistical mechanics and have been studied extensively. In this paper, we introduce a quantitative high-dimensional extension of this notion, called $δ$-ultra-log-concavity, for probability measures on $\mathbb{N}^d$ with downward closed support. When $δ= 1$, this notion coincides with the class studied by Gurvits (2009) via strongly log-concave generating functions, and with the class defined by Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant (2021) via completely log-concave generating functions; in one dimension, it reduces to classical ultra-log-concavity. We establish several functional inequalities, including a weighted Poincaré inequality, a discrete Brascamp--Lieb inequality, and a weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality. Our approach combines integrated Bakry--Émery calculus for a canonical birth-death chain with Poisson stochastic localization, which arises as the time reversal of coordinatewise binomial thinning. We further establish concentration of measure, maximum-entropy principles, and several closure properties for ultra-log-concave measures, and develop applications to queueing models, polymatroids, antiferromagnetic Potts models, and hardcore models. Finally, a lattice scaling limit of the discrete theory yields Poincaré and Brascamp--Lieb inequalities for Laguerre diffusions.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We show that given a log-concave offspring distribution, the corresponding sequence of Bienaymé-Galton-Watson trees conditioned to have $n\geq 1$ vertices admits a realization as a Markov process $(T_n)_{n\geq1}$ which adds a new ''right-leaning'' leaf at each step. This applies for instance to offspring distributions which are Poisson, binomial, geometric, or any convolution of those. By a negative result of Janson, the log-concavity condition is optimal in the restricted case of offspring distributions supported in $\{0,1,2\}$. We then prove a generalization to the case of an offspring distribution supported on an arithmetic progression, if we assume log-concavity along that progression. As an application, we deduce the existence of increasing couplings in an inhomogeneous model of random subtrees of the Ulam--Harris tree. This is equivalent to the statement that, in a corresponding inhomogeneous Bernouilli percolation model on a regular tree, the root cluster is stochastically increasing in its size. These results generalize a construction of Luczak and Winkler which applies to uniformly sampled subtrees with $n$ vertices of the infinite complete $d$-ary trees. Our proofs are elementary and we tried to make them as self-contained as possible.

editorial_contributions.text:
This research monograph is concerned with precise approximations to the process of component counts in random decomposable combinatorial structures by simpler discrete, independent processes. The authors develop powerful methods for pushing most of the results (as well as the conditions required) to their limit. The arguments used are completely probabilistic (unlike some of the authors' previous papers), and indeed the book may be roughly summarized as a deep study of component counts in decomposable combinatorial structures without generating function, without Fourier analysis, and with purely probabilistic reasoning.

A prototype of the so-called ``logarithmic combinatorial structures'' is cycles in permutations. Permutations can be viewed as a set of cycles, whose exponential generating function is of the form \(\log(1/(1-z))\) (since there are \((n-1)!\) different ways of arranging \(n\) distinct numbers in a cycle), thus the term ``logarithmic''. The authors' view of the cycle structures is through the fine, informative counting process \((C_1(n), C_2(n), \dots)\), where \(C_i(n)\) denotes the number of cycles of size \(i\) in a random permutation of \(n\) elements. The basic idea is that if we have good knowledge on such processes, then many other properties like the distribution of the total number of cycles and functional limit theorems can be derived. Two typical types of limit theorems are as follows. (i) \((C_1(n), C_2(n), \dots)\) converges in distribution to \((\text{Po}(1), \text{Po}(\frac 12), \dots)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_+^\infty\), where \(\text{Po}(\frac1i)\) denotes a Poisson random variable with mean \(1/i\), and, (ii) for the size of the \(k\)th largest cycle \(L_k(n)\), \(n^{-1} (L_1(n), L_2(n), \dots)\) converges in distribution to \((L_1, L_2, \dots)\) in \([0,1]^\infty\), where the random vector \((L_1, L_2,\dots)\) has a Poisson-Dirichlet distribution with parameter \(1\).

These results roughly say that counts of small cycles are asymptotically independent, while those of large cycles are strongly dependent. In this book such results are (i) extended to cover a wider class of combinatorial structures, and (ii) refined by stronger types of approximation theorems with different degrees of precision on error rate.

For a general treatment of the component counts, the following two conditions are crucial: (i) the conditioning relation 
\[
 \mathcal{L}(C_1^{(n)}, \dots,C_n^{(n)}) = \mathcal{L}(Z_1,\dots,Z_n \mid Z_1+2Z_2+\cdots + nZ_n =n), 
\]
 and (ii) the logarithmic condition 
\[
 \mathbb{P}(Z_n=1) \sim \mathbb{E}(Z_n) \sim \theta/n \qquad (\theta>0). 
\]
 Here \(C_j^{(n)}\) denotes the number of components of size \(j\) and the \(Z_j\)'s are some discrete random variables, which are usually Poisson, binomial or negative binomial. From a combinatorial point of view, the conditioning relation corresponds roughly to decomposability of the underlying structure and the logarithmic condition reflects analytic properties needed on the generating functions.

For the types of approximation theorems, the authors study mostly the total variation distances \(d_{\text{TV}}(\mathcal{L}(C_1^{(n)}, \dots,C_b^{(n)}), \mathcal{L}(Z_1,\dots,Z_b))\) and \( d_{\text{TV}}(\mathcal{L}(C_{b+1}^{(n)}, \dots,C_n^{(n)}), \mathcal{L}(C_{b+1}^{*(n)},\dots,C_n^{*(n)}))\), where \(d_{\text{TV}}\) denotes the total variation distance and \(C_j^{*(n)}\) denotes the numbers of cycles of lengths \(j\), in a \(\theta\)-biased random permutation of \(n\) objects (whose joint distribution follows the Ewens sampling formula). Once good bounds are available for these distances, properties for the approximators can be transferred to those of the component counts. Thus two chapters (4 and 5) are devoted to derive all types of properties needed for the Ewens sampling formula, which include local and functional limit theorems and large deviations for the number of cycles, distributions of the lengths of small cycles, ordered cycle lengths, and largest cycles, and the Erdős-Turán law for log order of a random element. The diversity of the types of results implied by the authors' strong approximation theorems shows the advantages of the authors' consideration of the more general total variation distances.

A large amount of fine estimates are derived in order to achieve the generality of the condition and the precision for the total variation distances. The first half of the book (first six chapters) describes the background, the main types of results discussed in the book, properties needed for the Ewens sampling formula (which is used later on as a basic approximator), as well as the methods of proof used. Chapter 7 describes the main theorems of the book under general conditions whose consequences are discussed in Chapter 8; the proofs are then given in Chapters 9 to 14 (pp.\ 225 -- 338).

The contents of each chapter are sketched as follows. Chapter 1 starts from a discussion of properties of cycles in permutations: joint distribution and moments of cycle counts (Cauchy's formula), marginal distribution, total variation distance between the cycle counts and Poisson process, the Feller coupling, local and functional limit theorems for total number of cycles, distributions of the small and large cycles, age-ordered list of cycle lengths, and the Erdős-Turán law. Then the asymptotic analogy between cycles in permutations and prime factors in random integers are highlighted (theory in one side is generally inspiring for that in the other). Chapter 2 describes decomposable combinatorial structures, aiming mainly at assemblies (set construction for labelled structures), multisets and selections (set construction for unlabelled structures), and their variations by refining, coloring and tilting, the viewpoint being consistently probabilistic. Examples include integer partitions, set partitions, polynomials over finite fields, binary search trees, additive arithmetic semigroups, coagulation fragmentation processes, etc. Chapter 3 gives an overview of the main results in the book, beginning with the conditioning relation and logarithmic condition. A section on total variation and Wasserstein distances and another on Stein's method are included. Chapters 4 and 5 give a detailed discussion of the Ewens sampling formula. The notion of size-biasing is first introduced. Chapter 4 then focusses on distributional properties of the random variables \(n^{-1} \sum_{b<j\leq n} jZ_j\), where \(\mathcal{L}(Z_j) =\mathcal{L}(\text{Po}(1/j))\), \(0\leq b<n\). The main reason of studying such partial sums is that the total variation distance between two random vectors are reduced to some weighted sum of two random variables (one-dimensional) of such a type. Chapter 5 then deals with the more general process approximations. Chapter 6 turns to general logarithmic combinatorial structures and follows the same pattern of treatment for Ewens sampling formula by considering first distributions of \(n^{-1}\sum_{b<j\leq n}jC_j^{(n)}\) and then the associated process approximations. It derives, in particular, asymptotics of the total variation distance between the process of component counts in assembly, multiset and selection constructions and the associated limiting process. From Chapter 7 on, the treatment is for more general (not only for assembly, multiset and selection) logarithmic structures but under stronger analytic assumptions in order to prove more effective bounds on the total variation distances. ``Chapter 8 gives a number of consequences of the approximation theorems of the preceding chapter, illustrating the power inherent in discrete functional limit theorems and approximations. Each is based on earlier limiting results, improving upon them in two ways. First, the context is broadened from an often quite restrictive setting to that of a very general logarithmic combinatorial structure. Secondly, the limit theorems are supplied with error bounds.''

This book, whose title was already cited in the paper by \textit{R. Arratia} and \textit{S. Tavaré} [Adv. Math. 104, 90--154 (1994; Zbl 0802.60008)], represents the culmination of a decade-long research by the authors. It is very well-written and informative. Highly recommended.

editorial_contributions.text:
An algorithm is proposed for the hypergeometric distribution and generalizations and limiting cases thereof: binomial, Poisson, Pascal \((=negative\) binomial), geometric, rectangular, and many more ``similar'' ones as e.g. logarithmic series, hyper-Poisson, Polya-Eggenberger. 


It is the rejection algorithm for generating random variates in the cases, when the distribution is discrete univariate, unimodal and not feasibly invertible (by computation), but closely majorized by an easily computable function g(k). Considered are distributions \(p_ k\) (k\(\in {\mathbb{Z}})\) with log \(p_ k\) concave and therefore of limited variance in k (uniformly), which covers the above mentioned distributions. In this case g(k) can be a constant or simple stepwise exponentially) decreasing function, i.e.: \(g(k)=c\cdot e^{-a| m-k|}\) for k outside the range of the modes (points with maximal probability, m one of them, c depending on the sign of m-k). On the other hand, for the rejection algorithm, the expected number of trials turns out to be \(4+p_ m\) (less in special cases), where \(p_ m\) is the probability of a mode. 


The algorithm itself is a simple program of a few lines - besides using a call for the actual distribution function - consisting of usual arithmetic, a call for the exponential (as being the principal part of the majoriser), three calls for generating independent random variables (uniform in 0...1), a call for a random sign \((+/-)\), and a combination of comparisons as rejection condition; all this for each trial. 


The performance depends on the closeness of g(k) to the actual distribution and is not discussed.

editorial_contributions.text:
The present book proposes a professional approach to the statistical theory from the computational and mathematical point of view, using the powerful computer software Mathematica as support for the advanced numeric and symbolic computations. Mathematica is not just a specialized statistical package (like SPSS, Gauss, Systat, SAS, S-Plus, etc.), but much more: Mathematica provides both a (arbitrary-precision) numerical engine and a powerful symbolic/algebraic engine oriented to problem solving in mathematical statistics. Mathematica is running on a wide variety of computer platforms; the present book is bundled with the special software package mathStatica, an add-on to Mathematica, a sophisticated toolset specially designed for doing mathematical statistics (enclosed on the two attached CD-ROMs). Addressed at researchers, students, and professional practitioners with a good knowledge of mathematical statistics, the focus of this book is on problem solving rather than mathematical theorems and proofs, using the mathStatica and Mathematica packages to bring mathematical statistics to real life.


The contents of the book are structured within 12 chapters, covering from elementary up to the highest-level topics, results and problems. Chapter 1 (Introduction) tells the reader how to install the enclosed Mathematica software, and provides the core functions, notations and conventions. Chapter 2 (Continuous Random Variables) shows mathStatica computing for various continuous measures of location (mean, mode, median and quantiles), moments and generating functions, conditional distributions and expectations, and pseudo-random number generation. Chapter 3 (Discrete Random Variables) turns the reader's attention toward experiments defined on countable (discrete) sample spaces. Various discrete random variables are examined, whose domain of support is the set of non-negative integers: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, geometric, negative binomial, and hyper-geometric distributions, as well as component-mixing and parameter-mixing distributions. Chapter 4 (Distributions of Functions of Random Variables) deals with an important practical problem: which is the distribution of a function applied to a random variable, whose density function is given? Two main approaches are experimented: the Transformation Method, and the MGF (moment generating function) Method. Chapter 5 (Systems of Distributions) discusses three systems of distributions: (1) the Pearson family, which defines a density in terms of its slope; (2) the Johnson system, describing density in terms of transformations of the standard normal; (3) Gram-Charlier expansions which represent a density as a series expansion of the standard normal density.


Chapter 6 (Mulivariate Distributions) provides the transition from univariate to multivariate statistical analysis, introducing and experimenting new concepts such as: joint densities, joint distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, multivariate expectations, product moments, etc., properties of dependence and independence, important multivariate distributions. Chapter 7 (Moments of Sampling Distributions) addresses two topics: (a) unbiased estimators of population moments, and (b) population moments of sample moments. Chapter 8 (Asymptotic Theory) investigates desirable asymptotic properties such as consistency and limiting normality, in the context of sample mean and sample sum (in the simple case of i.i.d. random variables). Chapter 9 (Statistical Decision Theory) examines how to select an estimator, in an optimal fashion, from the set of decisions. Loss and risk, mean square error as risk, and order statistics are the topics of computational experiments. In Chapter 10 (Unbiased Parameter Estimation), the statistical information that is present in a parameter in a statistical model is measured using Fisher information, sample information, etc., this leading to Cramér-Rao lower lower bound and best unbiased estimators. The theoretical development of Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimation (MVUE) is based on the famous theorem of Rao and Blackwell, in the context of MVUE sufficient statistics and its completeness. Chapter 11 (Principles of Maximum Likelihood Estimation) and Chapter 12 (Maximum Likelihood Estimation in Practice) propose interesting theoretical and applicational experiments related to ML (Maximum Likelihood) estimation based on the algorithms enclosed in the Mathematica and mathStatica packages. A useful Appendix ends the book. The bunch of exercises at the end of each chapter represents another argument to consider this book also a perfect companion to any kind of (universitary) course level in mathematical statistics.

editorial_contributions.text:
Because of the special place of probability and its applications in both modern science and the modern world, the necessity of such a dictionary in the English language is more than obvious. Hence, its appearance can and must be considered as an important event. Related to this work, there are the highest expectations by the probability community about the contents and the quality of such an edition.

Professor Stirzaker is known as author and co-author of books addressed mainly to students at different levels. Based on his rich experience, he has taken now a very ambitious task: to prepare the ``missing'' dictionary. Fundamentally, this is an excellent idea of both the author and the publisher.

In general, the dictionary is expected to be at the highest level of perfection. This means:

{\parindent=6mm \begin{itemize}\item[(1)] the chosen terms/items should represent comprehensively modern probability and its diverse applications; \item[(2)] the items should cover both classical concepts and results, and very recent developments; \item[(3)] the style should be smooth and guide the reader to the essence in a clear and convincing way; \item[(4)] to each item, the most appropriate references should be given; \item[(5)] the presentation and notation should follow the best international traditions and the design of the volume should be attractive. 

\end{itemize}}

It is positive that we find in the present dictionary much of the above mentioned. The dictionary contains a large number of items/terms. The main items, called `headwords', are about 3,000, and with additional terms discussed within the main ones, the total number is around 5,000. As it is explained, the items are from probability, stochastic processes and their applications in areas such as stochastic financial modelling and insurance, operations research, games and optimization, queuing and reliability theory, networks and communication theory.

The style is appropriate: to follow strictly the lexicographic order of the items, provide rigorous definitions, followed by essential properties and results, and provide at least one reference for each item. Rich cross-referencing reveals expected and unexpected connections between items or concepts.

The choice of items included is the most serious and not an easy task. It is also, at least partly, a matter of a personal judgment and taste. The items included in the dictionary are important and, in general, properly described.

Thus, several positive words can be said for this (first!) edition of the dictionary. However, it is more important to mention about what is missing and what is not well done.

Here is a short list of items whose description suffers of one or another kind of inaccuracy or incompleteness: `arcsin law' (p. 11, and other places, e.g., p. 42 involving a uniform r.v. \(U\)) -- since we still do not know how to divide by \(0\) (zero), it should be \(x \in (0,1),\) not \([0,1]\); it is the same, \(x \in (0,1),\) for the beta distribution, everywhere, not just once; the author writes consistently about the mgf, see, e.g., the items `complete convergence', `Coxian distribution', `Laplace transform', respectively, in pages 74, 90, 229. In page 91, `Cramér's condition', part 2, he adds that this is exactly the mgf. Improvements have to be made in `log gamma distribution' (p. 244), `marginal distribution' (p. 251), `Lévy-Khinchin formula', `collector problem' (p. 72), `Borel-Cantelli lemma', case (b) (p. 41), `concordance order' (p. 77), `sigma-field' (p. 344).

The Kolmogorov existence theorem is strangely enough omitted. There is no definition of \(n\)-dimensional distribution functions. To use \(n\)-dimensional df or multivariate df is more common than `joint distribution' used by the author.

Comparing the dictionary with other available sources, we see that there is a reasonable number of items which are important in modern probability but they are not included. Here is only a brief list (in arbitrary order): KAM theory, Sinai billiard, Lyapunov exponent, Lyapunov function, Bernstein polynomials, Kolmogorov-Obukhov \(5/3\) law, Poisson summation formula, random partition, quasimartingale, stochastic Navier-Stokes equation, Stefan problem, Krylov-Safonov theorem, Tsirelson example, Buffon-Sylvester problem, piecewise deterministic Markov process, Roberts-Shiryaev procedure, mean-median-mode inequality, Cacoullos inequality, Rossberg theorem, intermittency, non-central chi-squared distribution, evolution SDE, stochastic averaging method, Zvonkin theorem, Gaussian martingale, Hardy's condition, Stirling numbers, Baxter theorem, Pinelis inequality, Itô-Wentzell formula, semi-Markov process, Kakutani-Hellinger distance.

Regarding the references. The author says that the choice among `meritorious works' has been made randomly. This does not seem to be a good approach. Some references look strange, and it is easy to indicate good and appropriate sources. While most of the references are given correctly, it is disturbing to see incomplete data, inconsistencies or missing references at all. See, e.g., pages 43, 50, 68, 76, 88, 110, 113, 153, 158, 191, 193, 251, 300. By writing J. Kingman, we know who is behind this, but when writing G. Lin or Y. Wang, zbMATH tells us that there are several thousand. It is a standard to write all available initials of the cited authors. For some names, especially of Russian mathematicians, the author has chosen to use a version which unfortunately is not the best generally accepted. E.g., it should be `Chebyshev', and not the chosen `Chebyshov' (there is a funny typo in the verses cited in p. 63). What to say about the three different ways of writing the same name: Erdos, Erdös and Erdős? Or another name spelled in two ways: Itô and Itō?

Regarding the symbols and notation. It is expected the author to follow the best international traditions. In fact, most of the symbols and the notation in the dictionary are appropriately chosen and used. But not all. Here are just two exceptions.

First. Even for the very basic object, namely, the distribution function, the author uses \(F(x)\). The standard and correct way is to write only \(F\) knowing well that in fact, \(F=(F(x), \;x \in {\mathbb R})\), which obviously is an infinite and uncountable object, like any function defined on \(\mathbb R\). Notice, \(F(x)\) is a single real number in the interval \([0,1]\), the value of \(F\) at \(x\). To write \(F(x)\) for the whole distribution function is old fashioned and inadequate. Similar comments should be made also for characteristic functions \(\phi\).

Second. The author (like other authors) uses the font \(\mathbb {P, \, E}\) for `probability' and `expectation'. The same font is traditionally used for certain spaces, e.g., \({\mathbb {R, \, C}}\) for the real and complex numbers, respectively, and \({\mathbb {N, \, Z}}\) for sets of integers. In parallel with \({\mathbb N}\), the author uses the symbol \({\mathbb Z}^+\), however the latter is not in the list.

Notice, however, that as a group of objects (operations), probability, expectation and variance are very different from the group of objects consisting of spaces and sets. It is desirable to distinguish them visually.

The use of the same font for such different objects can be compared with an artist who uses in one painting the same colour for drawing the sky and the grass, or imagine that two football teams come to the field and all 22 players wear shirts of the same design and the same colour (only with different numbers and names, of course). Thus, a good alternative is any of the following three fonts: (a) \({\mathbf {P, \, E, \, V}}\); \, (b) \({\text{P, \, E, \, V}}\); \, (c) \({\mathsf{P, \, E, \, V}}\). Perhaps, the best is the third font (c), called `sans serif'. This appropriate font has been effectively used by many outstanding authors. Eventually, by using `sans serif', a future corrected edition of the dictionary definitely would have a modern and intelligent shape.

Some words about the abbreviations. Most of them are traditional. But not all of them. I wonder why the author did not write \(\Gamma (a)\) and \(\text{B}\) \((a,b)\) for the classical Euler gamma and beta functions, as it is done in thousands of books and papers. For the gamma and beta distributions, it is much better and absolutely appropriate to use, e.g., \(\gamma (m,\lambda)\) and \(\beta (a,b)\); or, if you wish, just use Gamma\((a,b)\) and Beta\((a,b)\). The latter would be of the same style as Ber\((p)\), Exp\((\lambda)\), Poi\((\lambda)\). The notation Bin\((n,p)\) for the binomial distribution is generally accepted and much better than just B\((n,p)\) used here.

There is no reason not to use `df' for `distribution function', instead of the old fashioned `cdf' for cumulative df. Hence `df' should appear in the list of abbreviations and be used everywhere. This would go well with `chf', `mgf', `pgf', etc.

When reading carefully the whole text, for more than a month, I have found a large number of other inconsistencies (not listed here), besides those commented above. Some of them are technical. The number of places needing to be corrected is more than 200. I am sure that other readers will also find places for correction, the same I have discovered or different ones.

I guess, the reason for all this is that after the author's submission, the text has not been reviewed by an independent professional. Also, it is not clear if any editor of CUP has been involved. Otherwise, the author would acknowledge such a work. Here, there is no acknowledgment.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: In this study, properties of Negative Binomial Distribution (NBD) are examined along with its mixture. NBD is a discrete probability distribution used to model the number of failures in a sequence of independently and identically distributed Bernoulli trials before a specified number of successes occur. The NBD provides an excellent model for a frequency distribution where the variance of the distribution is larger than the mean. The mixture of NBD, known as compound distribution, is a probability model that brings together NBD to fit data appropriately with varying dispersion, especially where the standard model is not sufficient on its own. It is used to model complex data and assumes that the data used is a weighted average of many sub-populations. The properties of NBD are examined with respect to the mode, truncation and Poisson distribution as limiting cases of NBD. Different forms of NBD in the likes of Anscombe, Pascal and their properties have been established. In conclusion, QNBD and its structural properties are obtained. Furthermore, mixtures of Negative Binomial Distribution in relation to gamma, Poisson and multivariable distributions are presented.

editorial_contributions.text:
Computational physics has been developed to an important part of natural and engineering sciences. Computer simulation of physical systems provides a deeper insight into the underlying theories and can be a starting point for new mathematical investigations too.

The well-written monograph about computational physics is based on two-semester lecture courses given by the author on a period of several years for undergraduate physics and biophysics students at the Technische Universität München. The book is also convenient for students and practitioners of computer science, chemistry, and mathematics who are interested in applications of numerical methods in physics and engineering sciences.

The 454 + xviii pages long monograph consists of prefaces to the first and second edition, 21 chapters, 2 appendices, 284 references and an index with relevant terms. The first part is devoted to the most important basic numerical methods which are used in the applications with a focus on the algorithms and the accuracy of the results mostly omitting proofs. The second part (9 chapters on 194 pages) is focused on computer simulation methods for selected applications of classical and quantum systems. Each chapter is finished by a section ``Problems'' with numerous examples giving a deeper insight into the algorithms and into the physical background as the case may be. Corresponding program examples are formulated as Java applets. The source codes can be downloaded from a web page and the reader can run the routines after compiling them on his own computer without programming skills. But, the interested reader can also modify the codes using the freely available programming environment ``netbean'', described in the appendix ``Performing the computer experiments''.

Compared to the first edition [Berlin: Springer (2010; Zbl 1251.82002)] the monograph is extended by the chapters ``Discretization of differential equations'' and ``Molecular dynamics'' but, also other chapters are changed and additional methods are included. All in all, the second edition contains 245 pages more in comparison to the first one.

In general it is not the aim of the author to present the recently best algorithm for a problem, rather prevalent methods are selected. In many cases, a range of methods is described and the reader has to make an appropriate choice for his own task. The appendix ``Methods and algorithms'' contains all the treated purposes and methods with a short description of their properties in a tabular form in order to help the user to select the appropriate algorithm. The arrangement of the chapters differs partly from conventional monographs about numerical mathematics and is more aligned with the physical applications.

Chapter 1 is devoted to error analysis. The limited precision of input data (experimental uncertainty), rounding and truncation errors have an impact on the accuracy of the numerical results. Starting from the fact that the arithmetic unit of a computer only works with a finite precision number (in general single, double and quadruple) the notion of `machine number' is introduced. The machine numbers can be considered as a subset of the real numbers. The corresponding IEEE standard is presented. The propagation of the errors in a sequence of elementary operations is outlined. Furthermore, truncation errors, e.g., caused by the approximation of series expansions, and stability problems of iterative algorithms are demonstrated in examples.

Chapter 2 treats the interpolation needed if a function is known only at a discrete set of data points and additional values have to be computed. An interpolation method is classified as linear if the interpolating function can be described as a linear sum of functions. The author introduces the linear interpolation using polynomials, trigonometric functions, or splines and the nonlinear interpolation with rational and exponential functions. The Lagrange and the barycentric Lagrange interpolation method, Newton's divided differences, Neville's method, and splines for long range interpolation are presented in detail as examples for the linear interpolation including an error estimation and hints in which situations the several methods should be used. Especially for the interpolation of functions with poles a rational interpolation is considered using the Padé approximation to a function. The author outlines also linear two-dimensional interpolation methods by polynomials and piecewise defined polynomials (splines). Trigonometric interpolation and curve fitting in general are included in the chapters Fourier transformation and Data fitting, respectively. In all cases the reader will find here and in the following chapters hints to additional literature.

The subject of Chapter 3, the numerical differentiation, is mainly required for the discretization of differential equations. The reader will find a short introduction into the forward and the symmetric central differential quotients including the error orders. The extrapolation method and the polynomial interpolation are introduced to obtain higher-order approximations. The construction of partial derivatives of multivariate functions is demonstrated for the case of two dimensions for nine sample points using Lagrange polynomials. The approximation of the gradient, of the Laplace operator, and of the mixed second derivative are presented.

Chapter 4 is devoted to the numerical integration of definite integrals over a finite interval. Integrals over an infinite interval can be treated by a preceding transformation to integrals over a finite interval. Generally, a definite integral is approximated by a set of quadrature points and weights. Using \(N+1\) equidistant points and the Lagrange interpolating polynomial of order \(N\) gives the so-called Newton-Cotes formulae (\(N = 1\): trapezoidal rule, \(N = 2\): Simpson's rule, \(N = 3\): 3/8 rule, and so on). The author presents closed, open, and composite Newton-Cotes rules. The accuracy of the methods can be improved by extrapolation. As an example, the Romberg integration is considered that needs many function evaluations but can be used to get results with nearly machine precision. Another method to rise the accuracy in comparison to the slowly convergent Newton-Cotes rules consists in the optimization of the positions of the quadrature points. The reader is introduced to the Clenshaw-Curtis and the Gaussian quadrature. The \(2N\) quadrature points and weights of the Gaussian integration are calculated in such a way that a polynomial of order \(2N-1\) is integrated exactly using orthogonal polynomials for the determination of the quadrature points and weights. The author presents several types of Gaussian quadrature depending on the kind of the used orthogonal polynomials (Legendre, Chebyshev, Hermite, and Laguerre polynomials). For the interested reader, the connection between the determination of the quadrature points and weights and a corresponding eigenvalue problem is outlined

Systems of inhomogeneous linear equations arising, e.g., from the discretization of differential equations or from a linearization of nonlinear equations, have to be solved often in the inner cycle of complex programs. Thus, efficient and accurate algorithms are needed for this linear algebra problem. Direct methods for low-dimensional systems and iterative algorithms for large-scale problems are treated in Chapter 5. The Gaussian elimination consisting of an \(LU\) decomposition and a backward substitution is presented, including remarks on pivoting (partial and total) and matrix balancing to improve the numerical stability. The specialized Gaussian elimination methods for tridiagonal and cyclic tridiagonal matrices are also described and avoid the storage of the zero elements and saves computing times. An alternative direct method to solve linear systems is the \(QR\) decomposition that is well appropriate for overdetermined systems, but the algorithm is formulated for \(n\times n\) matrices only. The Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization and Householder reflections are depicted to perform the \(QR\) decomposition. Both decompositions are also proposed for the matrix inversion.

The reviewer misses here and in the chapter about eigenvalue problems for these fundamental parts of numerical mathematics hints to efficient software solutions, such as LAPACK [\textit{E. Anderson} et al., LAPACK user's guide. Philadelphia, PA: SIAM, Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (1999; Zbl 0934.65030)] and the extensions ScaLAPACK for MIMD architectures (multiple instruction multiple data stream) and PLAPACK for general parallel computers, in which the algorithms are adapted by employing modern cache-based architectures and more general memory hierarchies, using basic Linear Algebra subprograms (BLAS, BLACS, and parallel BLAS) as interface between LAPACK and the different machine architectures.

For the solution of systems with large sparse matrices, iterative methods are presented. The reader is introduced into two relaxation methods, the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel method, dividing the original matrix into a diagonal and two triangular matrices. The convergence is improved by successive overrelaxation. Furthermore, the conjugate gradient method, convenient for symmetric positive matrices, is considered. The accuracy of the methods is outlined in the section `Problems' for well-conditioned (e.g., diagonal dominant symmetric matrices) and ill-conditioned matrices (e.g., Hilbert matrices).

A Krylov subspace method for large-scale nonsymmetric systems of linear equations and preconditioning techniques would be an enrichment in this field.

Chapter 6 is devoted to roots and extremal points in one dimension and in the multidimensional case.

Several algorithms with different features are presented for the one-dimensional case. The robust but slowly convergent bisection method and the regula falsi algorithm search the root of \(f(x)\) in a given interval with a sign change of \(f(x)\) at the interval end points. For functions that are differentiable at least two times, first- and second-order Newton-Raphson and secant methods are presented which converge fast if a good starting point is available. With a described interpolation method also complex roots can be calculated. Additionally, the reader will find root finding algorithms using inverse interpolation or combined methods, such as Dekker's and Brent's algorithm, joining the bisection and secant methods. Especially for high-order roots the author recommends Chandrupatla's method which uses inverse quadratic interpolation whenever possible.

The Newton-Raphson methods can be extended to the multidimensional root finding, with other words to the solution of systems of nonlinear equations in \(n\) variables. The user has to calculate the Jacobian matrix. This time-consuming calculation can be reduced by quasi-Newton methods applying an updating of the Jacobian matrix during the iterations. The update formula of Broyden and the Sherman-Morrison formula for the inverse Jacobian matrix are considered.

The derivatives of a function at the extremal points take the value zero. Thus, the minimization or maximization of differentiable functions can be done essentially applying root finding methods to the system of derivatives. Derivative-free methods have to be used if the function is not differentiable.

The ternary search and the golden section search method are introduced for unimodal functions. The steepest descent, conjugate gradient, the Newton-Raphson, and the quasi-Newton method are outlined for the multidimensional case.

The Fourier transformation is treated in Chapter 7. Goertzel's algorithm, the efficient fast Fourier transformation, and the trigonometric interpolation are considered.

There are a number of problems, such as the quadrature of high-dimensional integrals, many-body problems, problems in statistical thermodynamics, and in general in condensed matter physics and statistical mechanics, that cannot be solved by deterministic methods but, rather by Monte Carlo algorithms which sample the integration domain by randomly chosen points. One condition for the construction of a Monte Carlo method consists in the provision of random numbers with a given probability distribution. Chapter 8 is devoted to this part of numerical computation.

The author starts with basic ideas of statistics, such as the cumulative probability distribution, the histogram, and the moments (expectation value and variance). The Gaussian normal distribution, the binomial distribution, the probability density, and a central limit theorem are introduced. A multivariate distribution and the corresponding covariance matrix and correlation coefficient are considered for the case of two quantities.

Random numbers can be generated physically but, for computational methods, one generates pseudo-random numbers with similar statistical properties. The high-quality Marsaglia-Zamann random number generator is formulated including a C program and additional steps to get random numbers with a given distribution, thereof the Box-Muller method that generates Gaussian random numbers.

The Monte Carlo method is used for the calculation of \(\pi\) and of integrals. The Metropolis algorithm, an improved Monte Carlo method, is treated and it is shown how nonlinear optimization problems can be solved with it.

An important problem in physics consists in the solution of eigenvalue problems that is treated in Chapter 9. The representation is restricted to special (or ordinary) eigenvalue problems; general eigenvalue problems are not considered. The characteristic polynomial is introduced. The eigenvalues of the matrix are the roots of this polynomial and the corresponding eigenvectors can be found by solving a homogeneous system of linear equations. The method is only successful for matrices of small dimension. For real symmetric matrices of moderate dimension the Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm, which diagonalizes the matrix by a successive rotation of the coordinate system, and the reduction of the matrix to a symmetric tridiagonal matrix by a series of Householder transformations are described. The off-diagonal elements of the symmetric tridiagonal matrices are then eliminated applying a simplified \(QL\) algorithm. Discretizing second derivatives under Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions results in special tridiagonal matrices for which the author describes analytical solutions. Special methods are also given for matrices resulting from the symmetric difference quotient of a first derivative in one dimension and for a corresponding cyclic tridiagonal matrix. For the determination of some eigenvalues and eigenvectors of large-scale matrix eigenvalue problems the Lanczos algorithm is shortly outlined.

Chapter 10 is devoted to data fitting. In contrast to the interpolation with polynomials, splines or trigonometric functions already described in previous chapters, the given data points are only approximated by a continuous model function rather than to fit them exactly. The parameters of the model function have to be determinated such that the overall error of the residuals between the given data points and the corresponding function values is minimized. The error minimization based on the mean square difference results in the solution of the system of normal equations. The generally nonlinear problem (least squares fit) can be solved with methods described in Chapter 6. The normal equations are linear if the model function depends linearly on the parameters. Because of the high condition number of the normal matrix, the author proposes to orthogonalisize the rectangular matrix of the least squares problem using the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization method rather than to solve the normal equations directly by \(LU\) decomposition. Another topic of this chapter is the singular value decomposition that can be used, e.g., to approximate a high-dimensional rectangular matrix by a lower rank matrix with the aim to reduce redundancies. References are cited for applications in image compression, molecular dynamics, and bio-informatics.

Chapter 11 provides an overview on the discretization of differential equations. The considered methods are the discretization by finite differences, finite volumes, finite elements, spectral methods, weighted residual methods, and boundary element methods. The author starts with a classification of differential equations into ordinary and elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic, and ultra-hyperbolic partial differential equations including well-known examples from physics. Conservation laws are mentioned in connection with the advection, advection-diffusion, drift-diffusion, and the related Navier-Stokes equations.

Using a grid of equidistant points (regular grid) and approximating the differential operators in time and space as demonstrated in Chapter 3, finite difference methods are introduced, such as the forward-in-time centered-in-space scheme. Other topics are a stability analysis, the method of lines, and the solution by an eigenvector expansion.

Finite volume methods are based on average values of functions and derivatives over control volumes. Irregular grids are not a problem. In particular the discretization of fluxes (e.g., parts of hydro- and electrodynamic equations) is treated. Finite volume methods conserve the flux.

The next section focuses on weighted residual methods. Roughly speaking the solution is approximated by a linear combination of trial functions and the expansion is determinated such that the residuals become small, resulting in a finite system of equations or in a system of ordinary equations if the time is left continuous. The author describes the basic principles and properties of the point allocation, sub-domain, least squares, and Galerkin method.

Using basis functions, such as polynomials or Fourier sums that are nonzero in the whole domain, spectral and pseudo-spectral methods are outlined.

Dividing the integration volume into disjoint cells and using piecewise continuous polynomials as trial functions leads to the powerful finite element method (FEM). One-, two- and three-dimensional finite elements are considered. As an example the Galerkin FEM is demonstrated for a linear one-dimensional partial differential equation.

A short section is devoted to the boundary value method for linear partial differential equations for which a corresponding integral exists. Because only the surface of the integration volume has to be divided into the so-called boundary elements, one gets systems of linear equations smaller than that of the FEM but, in contrast to the FEM, with generally full corresponding coefficient matrix.

The headline of Chapter 12 reads as equations of motion. From a numerical point of view it could also be called numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). But the author focuses on the time evolution of the state vector described in a general equation of motion with the examples: motion of \(N\) interacting particles, diffusion equations, waves, and the Schrödinger equation for a two-level system. The reader will find short descriptions of nearly all important algorithms for initial value problems of ODEs, such as implicit and explicit methods, predictor-corrector methods, Runge-Kutta, extrapolations, multistep, and Verlet methods, without specifying them here. This chapter includes also discussions on adaptive step size control, error accumulation and stability problems.

Part II ``Simulation of classical and quantum systems'' starts with Chapter 13 ``Rotational motion''. A rigid body is defined as a set of mass points whose positions are given in a so-called ``laboratory coordinate system'' with the center of mass as origin. The rotation of the set relative to the laboratory system is described by a linear vector function with a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, the rotation matrix. The author deduces the properties of the rotation matrix, its connection with the vector of the angular velocity and its transformation properties. The total momentum and the angular momentum are defined. The equations of motion are formulated including those that describe the pure rotation of a rigid body, taking into account external forces. Practical algorithms for the solution of the equations of motion are discussed comparing them in several computer experiments from physics and proposing Omelyan's implicit quaternion method as very efficient algorithm that avoids the solution of nine equations with all its components and conserves the orthogonality of the rotation matrix.

The equations of motions play an important role in molecular mechanics simulations (Chapter 14) to investigate atomic and molecular systems. The atoms are considered as mass points that interact by classical forces that can be derived, e.g., from potential functions. Using three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates for \(N\) atoms results in a \(3N\)-dimensional system of equations of motion. For the consideration of molecule structures, atomic distances and angles have to be taken into account additionally. Typical force field terms are discussed, such as intramolecular and intermolecular contributions, as well as the computation of the gradients, e.g., for Coulomb and Lennard-Jones potentials. The special topic of this chapter, the nuclear motion around an equilibrium, is treated by an special eigenvalue problem (normal mode analysis). The equilibrium configurations can be determinated applying the algorithms of Chapter 6.

The equations of motion also act as a part in the calculation of thermodynamic averages in equilibrium systems. Therefore, a computer model of interacting particles is formulated as equation of motion with a force on an atom given by the gradient of the pairwise Lennard-Jones potential. The equations are solved using the Verlet method described in Chapter 12.

Another topic of this chapter is the calculation of the average magnetization in a magnetic field and the phase transition to the ferromagnetic state. The corresponding one- and two-dimensional Ising models are simulated using the Metropolis algorithm from Chapter 8.

Chapter 16 starts with random walks, defined as a sequence of random steps. The author studies discrete time random walks, the so-called discrete Markovian time models. Applying the central limit theorem to a random walk in one dimension, it is shown that the position of the walker after \(n\) steps approximates a Gaussian distribution. The shape configuration of a polymer is modeled by a 3-dimensional random walk consisting of a freely joint chain with constant bond length or using Hookian springs in a computer experiment. Another topic is the consideration of the motion of a heavy particle in a bath of smaller particles, the Brownian motion, by the Langevin model, in which the force caused by the collision with the lighter particles is described by a macroscopic average friction force.

Chapter 17 is devoted to electrostatics. The electrostatic potential of a charge distribution obeys the Poisson equation for a spatially varying permittivity or the Poisson-Boltzmann equation for mobile charges. The equations are discretized by the finite volume and boundary element methods described in Chapter 11.

Chapter 18 focuses on two types of classical waves, the electromagnetic waves and the mechanical waves. The one-dimensional wave equation is deduced from Maxwell's equations in the case of electromagnetic waves and from Euler's equation for an acoustic wave resulting in the same formal structure. Several methods are treated for the numerical solution of the wave equation, such as the reduction to systems of ordinary differential equations and the reduction of the second-order equation to two first-order PDEs. The leapfrog, the Lax-Wendroff, and the Crank-Nicolson (CN) scheme are presented for the solution of the first-order equations including the stability of the CN method for Courant numbers \(\alpha > 1\).

The transport of heat or the change of concentrations are described by the diffusion equation in Chapter 19. The properties of the explicit and implicit Euler and of the Crank-Nicolson method are discussed for the one-dimensional diffusion equation including an error analysis. The three-dimensional diffusion equation is split in such a way that the one-dimensional methods can be used independently for each dimension.

Nonlinear problems are the subject of Chapter 20, in particular recurrence relations, ordinary and partial differential equations, in which the included functions are nonlinear. Starting with iterated functions the ideas of orbits, fixed points (especially attractive, stable and higher-order fixed points), attractive and periodical cycles, chaotic behavior, bifurcation, and the Lyapunov exponent are introduced, well illustrated, and demonstrated by a model of population growth, the logistic map by Verhulst.

The iterated functions have to be replaced by an ordinary differential equation or systems of ordinary equations if the time is considered to be a continuous variable. Then the equilibrium assumes the role of fixed points. A stability analysis is executed for the continuous logistic model and predator-prey models by Lotka-Volterra and Holling-Tanner.

The next step consists in the simultaneous consideration of continuous time and spatial inhomogeneity. Investigated are reaction-diffusion systems and the Lotka-Volterra model with diffusion with the phenomena of pattern formation and traveling waves.

The last chapter is devoted to simple quantum systems. The numerical solution of the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation is discussed. The solution of this equation describes a particle by a wave packet in a potential. The numerical solution requires the time integration of the time evolution operator and the discretization of the second derivative for the kinetic energy. A number of methods (explicit and implicit Euler, Crank-Nicolson, second-order differencing, and split-operator methods) and their properties (stability, norm conservation of the wave function) are treated for the approximation of the time propagator. Pseudo-spectral methods and finite difference methods (3-point, 5-point and 7-point expression) are discussed for the spatial discretization. The application of the numerical methods is demonstrated for two-level systems and dissipative two-state systems. Topics are, e.g., the superexchange model, the ladder model, the Landau-Zener model, the Bloch equations, and the elementary qubit manipulation.

To sum up: this is very comprehensive and well-organized book with a concentration to the important ideas of the methods and physical applications including software, examples, illustrations, and references to further reading.

title.title: Log-concavity, ultra-log-concavity, and a maximum entropy property of discrete compound Poisson measures

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Ultra-log-concave distributions are ubiquitous in probability, combinatorics, and statistical mechanics and have been studied extensively. In this paper, we introduce a quantitative high-dimensional extension of this notion, called $δ$-ultra-log-concavity, for probability measures on $\mathbb{N}^d$ with downward closed support. When $δ= 1$, this notion coincides with the class studied by Gurvits (2009) via strongly log-concave generating functions, and with the class defined by Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant (2021) via completely log-concave generating functions; in one dimension, it reduces to classical ultra-log-concavity. We establish several functional inequalities, including a weighted Poincaré inequality, a discrete Brascamp--Lieb inequality, and a weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality. Our approach combines integrated Bakry--Émery calculus for a canonical birth-death chain with Poisson stochastic localization, which arises as the time reversal of coordinatewise binomial thinning. We further establish concentration of measure, maximum-entropy principles, and several closure properties for ultra-log-concave measures, and develop applications to queueing models, polymatroids, antiferromagnetic Potts models, and hardcore models. Finally, a lattice scaling limit of the discrete theory yields Poincaré and Brascamp--Lieb inequalities for Laguerre diffusions.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Motivated by a question of Krzysztof Oleszkiewicz we study a notion of weak tail domination of random vectors. title.title: Some stochastic inequalities for weighted sums

editorial_contributions.text:
Given a random variable \(X\), the concentration function is defined by
\[
Q(X;\lambda)=\sup_x\mathbb{P}(x\leq X\leq x+\lambda)
\]
for \(\lambda\geq0\), with the special case at \(\lambda=0\) of
\[
M(X)=Q(X;0)=\sup_x\mathbb{P}(X=x)\,.
\]
The authors aim to establish two-sided bounds for \(Q(X;\lambda)\) in the case where \(X\) is supported on the integers and has a log-concave distribution. In this setting, they show that
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+12\mbox{Var}(X)}}\leq M(X)\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+4\mathrm{Var}(X)}}\,,
\]
where the log-concavity is used only in the upper bound. Using the observation that \(Q(X;\lambda)=(\lambda+1)M(X+U_\lambda)\) for \(\lambda=0,1,2,\dots\), where \(U_\lambda\) is uniformly distributed on \(\{0,1,\dots,\lambda\}\), this then yields a two-sided bound on \(Q(X;\lambda)\) for integer-valued and log-concave \(X\). Analogous bounds for the Rényi entropy are also given, and these are used to establish versions of the entropy power inequality in the discrete log-concave setting. The paper concludes with an illustrative application to Bernoulli sums.

title.title: Dimension-free bounds for sums of independent matrices and simple tensors via the variational principle

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: Low-degree polynomial approximations to the sign function underlie pseudorandom generators for halfspaces, as well as algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. We study the limits of these constructions by proving inapproximability results for the sign function. First, we investigate the derandomization of Chernoff-type concentration inequalities. \textit{J. Schmidt} et al. [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 8, No. 2, 223--250 (1995; Zbl 0819.60032)] showed that a tail bound of \(\delta\) can be established for sums of Bernoulli random variables with only \(O(\log(1/\delta))\)-wise independence. We show that their results are tight up to constant factors. Secondly, the ``polynomial regression'' algorithm of \textit{A. T. Kalai} et al. [SIAM J. Comput. 37, No. 6, 1777--1805 (2008; Zbl 1155.68030)] shows that halfspaces can be efficiently learned with respect to log-concave distributions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) in the challenging agnostic learning model. The power of this algorithm relies on the fact that under log-concave distributions, halfspaces can be approximated arbitrarily well by low-degree polynomials. In contrast, we exhibit a large class of non-log-concave distributions under which polynomials of any degree cannot approximate the sign function to within arbitrarily low error.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1329.68027].

editorial_contributions.text:
Consider a random vector \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\), and a point \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\) on the unit sphere \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), that is, such that \(\theta_1^2+\cdots+\theta_n^2=1\). In this book the authors study approximation and concentration results for the sum
\[
\langle X,\theta\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^n\theta_k X_k
\]
and its corresponding distribution function \(F_\theta\). \textit{V. N. Sudakov} [Sov. Math., Dokl. 19, 1578--1582 (1978; Zbl 0416.60005)] observed that under mild conditions on \(X\) and for large \(n\), most (in the sense of normalised Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\)) of these distribution functions \(F_\theta\) are concentrated around a typical distribution function \(F\) given by \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}_\theta F_\theta(x)\), where \(\mathbb{E}_\theta\) is the integral with respect to the normalised Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\). This \(F\) may itself be close to the Gaussian distribution function \(\Phi\). The authors study concentration and large deviations bounds for \(F_\theta\), and explicit bounds on \(\mathbb{E}_\theta d(F_\theta,F)\) and \(\mathbb{E}_\theta d(F_\theta,\Phi)\) for a variety of metrics \(d\), including the Kolmogorov (uniform), Lévy, \(L^1\) and \(L^2\) distances.

This book is relatively self-contained, and assumes only familiarity with basic probability and analysis, making it suitable for use as the basis of a graduate-level course or reading group. Part I contains background in probability theory necessary for the more advanced parts of the text, including Khinchine-type inequalities, correlation conditions, log-concave distributions, Berry-Esseen-type inequalities, probability metrics, Rosenthal-type inequalities, and approximations and higher-order expansions for sums of independent random variables.

In Part II the authors give general results on concentration in Euclidean and abstract metric spaces, such as Poincaré-type inequalities (including results related to concentration, weighted versions and Brascamp-Lieb inequalities), Cheeger-type inequalities and log-Sobolev inequalities, together with examples. Topics covered here also include relative entropy and supremum- and infimum-convolution inequalities.

Following this more general introduction to concentration of measure, Part III introduces concentration results on the sphere \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) equipped with the Lebesgue measure. This includes inequalities of the types discussed above, concentration and large deviations results under various conditions, and Gaussian approximations and higher-order expansions for linear functionals.

In Part IV the authors discuss Sudakov's result, including rates of approximation in various metrics (both upper and lower bounds), and the proximity of \(F_\theta\) to Gaussian. They explore the structure of the typical distribution function \(F\), the characteristic function of \(F_\theta\), and concentration properties of \(F\) and \(F_\theta\). Bounds are given in the \(L^1\), Lévy and Kolmogorov distances, with refinements under the assumption of log-concavity of the distribution of \(X\).

Further bounds in Sudakov's result and Gaussian approximation are studied in Part V. Estimates in \(L^2\) distance are given via the Plancherel theorem. Conditions are given under which the Kolmogorov distance between \(F_\theta\) and \(\Phi\) has an improved rate of \(1/n\), up to logarithmic terms, compared to the rate \(1/\sqrt{n}\) that is typically observed. Relationships between the Kolmogorov and \(L^2\) distances are explored and corresponding lower bounds given.

Part V has a chapter giving examples and applications with specific classes of random variables \(X\), including trigonometric systems, the Walsh system on the discrete cube, empirical measures, and lacunary systems. Symmetric distributions are also discussed, including cases in which improved rates of convergence can be obtained, and further refinements under assumptions of log-concavity. Particular attention is paid to the case where \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent, including the study of Edgeworth expansions and conditions for improved rates. Finally, the authors also study cases in which \(\theta\) has special structure, including random sums and the case of Bernoulli coefficients in which \(\theta_k=\pm1/\sqrt{n}\) for all \(k\).

The exposition in the book is careful and thorough, with proofs given throughout. Each chapter concludes with remarks to give context, references and recent developments in the topic at hand, making this an excellent starting point for a study of the randomised sums considered here. While they begin with fundamental results in the area, the authors move carefully and efficiently to state-of-the-art techniques and results. Overall, this is a well-written book that will prove invaluable to researchers in the area.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper considers a problem of sampling from a strongly log-concave density in \(\mathbb R^d,\) and proves that an information theoretic lower bound on the number of stochastic gradient queries of the log density is needed.

It is achieved by applying several popular sampling algorithms (including many Markov chain Monte Carlo methods) by using stochastic gradients of the log density to generate a sample. The results of the paper establish an information theoretic limit for all these algorithms.

editorial_contributions.text: In [in: Contributions to probability, Collect. Pap. dedic. E. Lukacs, 201--206 (1981; Zbl 0534.60020)], \textit{L. A. Shepp} and \textit{I. Olkin} formulated the following conjecture: the Shannon entropy of a sum of independent heterogeneous Bernoulli random variables (that is a Poisson binomial random variable) is a concave function in the parameters of respective Bernoulli distributions. They have shown that this property is true for some particular cases. In the present paper, this subtle conjecture is fully proved. For the proof, the authors use a refined technique. Note that, the same authors have previously solved the `monotone' case of the Shepp-Olkin entropy concavity conjecture [\textit{E. Hillion} and \textit{O. Johnson}, Ann. Probab. 44, No. 1, 276--306 (2016; Zbl 1348.60139)]. The result on Shannon entropy is then extended to the entropy in the meanings of Rényi and of Tsallis.

editorial_contributions.text:
The aim of this paper is to review some results concerning the construction of interpolating families between finitely supported probability measures on a graph using the optimal transportation methods. Most of these results made the content of the following three papers previously published by the author [Potential Anal. 41, No. 3, 679--698 (2014; Zbl 1305.60014); Electron. J. Probab. 19, Paper No. 92, 29 p. (2014; Zbl 1347.49077); ``Entropy along \(W_{1;+}\)-geodesics on graphs'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1406:5089}]. The paper under review mainly focuses on the simpler case when the underlying graph is \( \mathbb{Z}\) and explains briefly how these constructions can be extended to the general case. Section 5 is dedicated to the case of entropic interpolations, along which concavity of entropy results hold. The paper ends by explaining how ideas coming from the optimal transportation theory on \(\mathbb{Z}\) can be used to solve the Shepp-Olkin conjecture concerning the concavity of the entropy of sums of independent Bernoulli random variables.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1377.52002].

title.title: Interpolation of probability measures on graphs

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Ultra-log-concave distributions are ubiquitous in probability, combinatorics, and statistical mechanics and have been studied extensively. In this paper, we introduce a quantitative high-dimensional extension of this notion, called $δ$-ultra-log-concavity, for probability measures on $\mathbb{N}^d$ with downward closed support. When $δ= 1$, this notion coincides with the class studied by Gurvits (2009) via strongly log-concave generating functions, and with the class defined by Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant (2021) via completely log-concave generating functions; in one dimension, it reduces to classical ultra-log-concavity. We establish several functional inequalities, including a weighted Poincaré inequality, a discrete Brascamp--Lieb inequality, and a weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality. Our approach combines integrated Bakry--Émery calculus for a canonical birth-death chain with Poisson stochastic localization, which arises as the time reversal of coordinatewise binomial thinning. We further establish concentration of measure, maximum-entropy principles, and several closure properties for ultra-log-concave measures, and develop applications to queueing models, polymatroids, antiferromagnetic Potts models, and hardcore models. Finally, a lattice scaling limit of the discrete theory yields Poincaré and Brascamp--Lieb inequalities for Laguerre diffusions.

title.title: High-Dimensional Ultra-Log-Concave Distributions
